segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's design the dispatch system for a ride hailing service, matching riders to nearby drivers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The core loop is location ingestion, proximity search, matching, and then trip state management until completion.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Start with location updates. Every active driver reports position every few seconds, which is a very high write rate.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: With a million active drivers reporting every four seconds, that is two hundred fifty thousand writes per second just for positions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should not write those to a durable transactional store. Current position belongs in memory with a short expiry.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The historical trail can go to a separate append only pipeline for analytics, billing and dispute resolution.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That separation is important. The real time path needs speed, the historical path needs durability, and they have different shapes.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Now the geospatial query. Given a rider's coordinates, find available drivers within a few kilometers, ranked by estimated arrival time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The classic approach is a geohash, which encodes latitude and longitude into a string where shared prefixes mean spatial proximity.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So we index drivers by geohash prefix and query the rider's cell plus the eight surrounding cells to avoid boundary misses.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The boundary problem is real. Two points can be a few meters apart but sit in different cells with completely different prefixes.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Hierarchical cell systems like S2 or the hexagonal H3 grid handle this more gracefully and give better shaped cells.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Hexagons have the nice property that all six neighbors are equidistant, which makes ring queries cleaner than with squares.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Whatever the grid, we keep an in memory index from cell identifier to the set of drivers currently in that cell.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: On each position update we move the driver between cells, which is two set operations rather than a full spatial rebuild.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Cell size is a tuning decision. Too large and every query scans thousands of drivers, too small and we query many cells.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Dense city centers and sparse suburbs argue for different sizes, which is why a hierarchical system with variable resolution helps.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Once we have candidates, straight line distance is a poor ranking signal because of rivers, highways and one way streets.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Agreed. We should use a routing engine to compute actual travel time for the shortlisted candidates, not for all of them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So filter geometrically to maybe twenty candidates, then compute real estimated arrival times for those, then rank.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Now the matching decision itself. The greedy approach assigns the nearest driver to each request as it arrives.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Greedy is simple but globally suboptimal. Two requests can each grab a driver in a way that leaves a third rider stranded.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Batched matching collects requests over a short window, a few seconds, and solves an assignment problem across the whole batch.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That typically reduces total wait time meaningfully, at the cost of adding the batching delay to every request.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The optimization objective is interesting. Minimizing total pickup time is not the same as minimizing the worst wait.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And neither accounts for fairness to drivers, or for repositioning supply toward areas where demand is about to rise.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's talk about the offer protocol. We send the trip to a driver, who has a limited time to accept.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: During that window the driver must be soft locked, otherwise a concurrent match could offer the same driver two trips.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A short lease in the dispatch store, with the driver marked as pending, handles that cleanly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: If the driver declines or the lease expires, we release them and offer the trip to the next candidate.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should cap the number of sequential offers, because a rider waiting through ten declines has a terrible experience.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: After a few failures we should widen the search radius rather than continuing to cycle within the same candidate set.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Trip state management comes next. A trip moves through requested, matched, en route, in progress and completed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Those transitions must be idempotent and recorded durably, because mobile clients on bad networks will retry everything.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Each transition should carry the expected current state, so a duplicate or out of order message is rejected safely.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For the live tracking during a trip, we push driver positions to the rider over a persistent connection.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We can reduce that traffic by sending the route once and then sending only position deltas along it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Clients can also interpolate between updates, which makes the marker move smoothly at a much lower update rate.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's discuss surge pricing, since it is really a supply and demand balancing mechanism rather than a pricing feature.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We compute the ratio of open requests to available drivers per geographic cell over a rolling window.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: When demand outpaces supply, the multiplier rises, which suppresses some demand and attracts drivers from adjacent areas.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The multiplier must be smoothed over time, otherwise it oscillates wildly and both riders and drivers lose trust in it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And the quoted price should be locked at request time, so a rider is never charged more than what they accepted.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: On the geographic architecture, this system partitions naturally by city or region, which is a big advantage.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A trip almost never crosses regional boundaries, so each region can run an independent dispatch cluster with its own state.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That limits the blast radius of failures and lets us deploy changes city by city rather than globally.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For failure handling, if the dispatch service loses its in memory index, drivers repopulate it within a few seconds of position updates.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: In flight trips are the harder case, so active trip state must live in durable storage, not only in memory.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A trip in progress must survive any service restart, because a rider physically in a car cannot simply be forgotten.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: To summarize, in memory geospatial index with hierarchical cells, routing based ranking of a small candidate set, and batched matching.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Plus leased offers, idempotent durable trip state, smoothed surge by cell, and regional partitioning for isolation.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The physical world constraints are what make this different. Real roads, real time and real people waiting on a curb.
